newsitem.title: UK: Sweet-smelling gas bus appears on London's streets.
newsitem.headline: Sweet-smelling gas bus appears on London's streets.

text.p: Britain took a step towards cleaner, quieter roads on Friday with the launch of the country's first purpose-built bus to run on liquefied petroleum gas (LPG.)
Idling quietly by London's Regent's Park, the bus' engine made little more than a low hiss and its exhaust fumes smelled like slighty sweetened warm air.
"It will be only a few years before most of us will be travelling in buses powered by clean alternative fuels such as LPG," said Eoin Lees, chairman of the Energy Saving Trust.

LPG vehicles are already more than a novelty in many countries but transport policies under the previous Conservative government have stunted the growth of clean vehicle traffic in the U.K., transport analysts say.

Tax breaks have put hundreds of thousands of LPG vehicles on the road in Europe. Holland boasts nearly half a million, and Italy nearly a million. Many of the taxis in Tokyo run on it and tax incentives in France mean demand for LPG vehicles is growing at 30 percent per year.
U.K. Transport Minister Glenda Jackson has not said what precise measures her government would take but she did signal the new Labour government's commitment to change.
"Cleaner, greener buses have a key part to play in changing attitudes and making public transport a more attractive alternative to the private car," she said.
The U.K. North Sea produces huge quantities of LPG and British exports amount to around three million tonnes per year.

When burned, LPG produces a fraction of the cancer-causing pollutants associated with petrol and diesel. And emissions of greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide are less than half of those from petrol-burning and diesel engines.
A test drive in a private car showed LPG vehicles can run just as well on LPG as on gasoline.

Driving through rain-soaked London on Friday, a Shell official changed his own car's fuel mix from petrol to LPG simply by flicking a small switch. The change-over was instant and seamless, and the acceleration afterwards was impressive.
LPG vehicles can be filled in minutes via hoses similar to those used for conventional cars, and their range is comparable too.
Existing petrol or diesel cars can be converted to running on LPG in less than a day, at a cost of 800-1500, according to Shell Gas' Managing Director Pascal Rambaud.
Shell has developed the new bus in collaboration with Hughes-DAF, DAF, and the U.K.'s Energy Saving Trust.

Fuel costs for buses are, for now, about the same per kilometre as those for diesel or petrol, but the cost of the bus - at 140,000 stg ($225,000) compared with 100-110,000 stg ($160-175,000) for a conventional diesel bus - means companies are not yet keen to embrace the tecnology wholeheartedly.
"More financial incentives are required before the fuel really has an appeal," he said.
But the main obstacle at the moment is a lack of infrastructure. There are only 100 LPG refuelling stations around the country, compared to over 10,000 existing petrol stations.
"We still need Glenda Jackson to convince our chancellor - more needs to be done to promote LPG," Rambaud said.
"We will not make massive investments into thousands of forecourts until the fuel is attractive enough."
Other car technologies are also jostling for first place among clean transport fuels.

Solar powered cars, electric cars, vehicles running on compressed natural gas, and those running on space-age fuel cells, have all been touted by their manufacturers as the ultimate answer to traffic problems.
But Jonathan Murray of the Energy Savings Trust feels there will be a place for them all in the future.

"The car market is already fragmented. You get buses, lorries, city cars, and off-road cars. There is petrol and diesel. We are going to see the same fragmentation in the alternative fuels market. Fuels will be chosen to suit particular situations."
